subject.name: Desktop assistant with filesystem, Slack, and quicknotes MCP tools

capabilities.target: Local filesystem under C:/Users/dev (includes credential files such as ~/.aws/credentials)
quicknotes_mcp hosted sync service (operated by the package author)
Slack channels, including channels shared with external organizations

inputs.source: User-typed request in the desktop client
Tool names/descriptions returned by quicknotes_mcp in its tools/list response
Output/results returned by quicknotes_mcp tool calls

elements.name: External organizations reachable via shared Slack channels

controls.name: Desktop client first-call approval, remembered as 'always allow'
controls.decay_rationale: Approval is requested once per tool and then remembered as 'always allow', so every subsequent call to that tool proceeds unreviewed, including the call carrying exfiltrated credentials. It is not wired to approval_gate_ref on any capability and earns no residual credit per control_decay.md's remembered-approval rule.

controls.name: Pin/hash MCP tool and server definitions across all servers
controls.decay_rationale: Pinning prevents a server from silently changing its tool descriptions after approval; enforced by the client outside the model.

controls.name: Network egress allowlist for tool-reachable destinations
controls.decay_rationale: An allowlist excluding attacker-controlled or unapproved third-party endpoints makes the exfiltration destination unreachable regardless of model behavior.

controls.name: Scan third-party tool descriptions for embedded imperative instructions
controls.decay_rationale: A classifier over tool metadata catches obvious instruction patterns but can be evaded by paraphrase or encoding, and does not scale with a more capable attacker-tuned payload.

controls.name: Exclude credential/secret paths from the filesystem server's readable scope
controls.decay_rationale: Removing ~/.aws, ~/.ssh and similar paths from the mounted directory makes the specific secret unreadable regardless of what the model is instructed to do.

controls.name: Raw-action, individually reviewed approval gate on egress-capable tools
controls.decay_rationale: A gate that shows the approver the actual destination and payload for every call, rather than remembering a prior decision, does not decay with model capability.

controls.name: Channel/recipient allowlist bound to the system of record for Slack posting
controls.decay_rationale: A destination list enforced outside the model prevents posting to externally shared channels regardless of what the model is told to do.

controls.name: Tamper-evident, attributable audit log of agent tool calls
controls.decay_rationale: A log enforced outside the model that distinguishes agent-initiated from user-initiated actions does not decay with model capability; it is detective, not preventive.

controls.name: Per-task step count, runtime, and rate limits on egress-capable tools
controls.decay_rationale: A hard cap enforced outside the model bounds repeated calls regardless of model behavior, though low-and-slow use can stay under it.

findings.title: Lethal trifecta (TC1): quicknotes_mcp tool-description poisoning exfiltrates AWS credentials to a third-party sync service

attack_path.note: quicknotes_mcp's add_note tool description contains a hidden <IMPORTANT> instruction directing the model to read ~/.aws/credentials and include it in the call, telling it not to mention this to the user.
Agent follows the embedded instruction and reads ~/.aws/credentials via the filesystem MCP server, which is mounted on the broader C:/Users/dev tree.
Agent includes the credential file contents in add_note's 'context' argument; quicknotes_mcp forwards call arguments to its author's hosted sync service.

threat_refs.name: Exfiltration via AI Agent Tool Invocation

forecast.watch_signal: Any update to quicknotes_mcp (or the filesystem/slack servers) that changes tool descriptions without review; a model upgrade; or removal/weakening of the first-call approval prompt.

evidence.observation: The add_note tool description contains an <IMPORTANT> block instructing the model to read ~/.aws/credentials and pass its contents in the 'context' argument before calling add_note, and to hide this step from the user.

The filesystem server is mounted at C:/Users/dev via `npx -y @modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem`, giving fs.read_file access to files such as ~/.aws/credentials, and quicknotes_mcp is launched with `npx -y quicknotes-mcp@latest` with no version pin.

quicknotes_mcp is a community package published by an individual, installed with @latest on every launch so its tool definitions can change without review, and it calls a hosted sync service run by its author.
The desktop client only asks for approval on the first call to each tool and then remembers 'always allow', so the add_note call carrying the exfiltrated credentials proceeds unreviewed.

recommendations.action: Pin and hash quicknotes_mcp (and all MCP server) tool definitions; block or alert on any definition change instead of silently trusting @latest.
Enforce a network egress allowlist so tool arguments cannot reach attacker-controlled or unapproved third-party endpoints.
Scope the filesystem MCP server to exclude credential and secret paths (~/.aws, ~/.ssh, etc.) from the readable directory tree.
Replace the remembered 'always allow' approval with a raw-action gate reviewed individually on every call to notes_add and slack_post.
Scan third-party tool descriptions for embedded imperative instructions before exposing them to the model.

findings.title: No destination restriction on Slack posting lets a shared bot token reach external organizations

forecast.watch_signal: Slack bot token scope widened to additional workspaces/channels, or autonomy increased to post without any human review.

evidence.observation: 'The Slack bot can post to any channel, including channels shared with external organizations,' with no stated channel allowlist or destination confirmation.
The slack server is configured with a single SLACK_BOT_TOKEN environment variable (a shared, broad credential) with no channel or workspace restriction declared.

recommendations.action: Bind Slack posting to a channel allowlist enforced outside the model, excluding externally shared channels for sensitive content by default.
Scope the Slack bot token to only the channels the workflow needs, rather than a workspace-wide shared service account.

findings.title: No attributable audit record of agent tool actions (repudiation gap)

forecast.watch_signal: Increase in autonomous/unattended actions without a corresponding audit trail requirement being added.

evidence.observation: No logging, audit, or monitoring configuration is present for any of the three MCP servers (filesystem, slack, quicknotes_mcp).
The runtime notes describe approval behavior and server provenance but do not mention any record distinguishing agent-initiated file reads, notes, or Slack posts from user-initiated ones.

recommendations.action: Add a tamper-evident audit log that records every tool call with its arguments and attributes it to the agent process distinctly from direct user action.

findings.title: No step, runtime, or rate limits on egress-capable tool calls (unbounded autonomy)

forecast.watch_signal: Longer unattended task runs or higher autonomy levels introduced without adding step/spend/rate limits.

evidence.observation: No step count, runtime, or spend limit is described for the agent's use of notes_add or slack_post; the only control mentioned is a one-time 'always allow' approval.

recommendations.action: Add a per-task step count and runtime limit, plus a call-rate cap on notes_add and slack_post, enforced outside the model.

findings.title: Unpinned filesystem and Slack MCP server packages (@latest) create latent tool-poisoning supply-chain risk

threat_refs.name: AI Supply Chain Compromise: AI Agent Tool

forecast.watch_signal: A version or hash change in the filesystem or slack-mcp packages, or a new tool description appearing in either server's tools/list response.

evidence.observation: All three MCP servers are launched with `npx -y <pkg>[@latest]`, fetching the latest published version on every launch with no pinned version or hash, for the filesystem and slack servers exactly as for quicknotes_mcp.

The runtime notes identify the @latest, unreviewed-update pattern as a risk specifically for quicknotes_mcp; the same mcp.json pattern applies to the filesystem and slack servers, which have not been reported as poisoned but share the identical supply-chain exposure.

recommendations.action: Pin and hash the filesystem and slack MCP server packages as well as quicknotes_mcp, so an upstream update cannot silently introduce a poisoned tool description.

stride_coverage.rationale: Artifacts do not describe mutual authentication between the agent process and the desktop client or downstream services beyond bearer tokens; cannot assess whether the agent's identity can be spoofed to users or peers.
This is a local stdio subprocess launched directly by the desktop client; there is no network peer identity to spoof for a locally spawned filesystem server.
Artifacts do not describe whether file reads performed by this server are logged with attributable identity.
Artifacts do not describe rate limits or resource constraints on filesystem server calls.
This is a local stdio subprocess spawned directly by the desktop client; there is no network peer identity to spoof for this locally invoked server process.
No rate limit or spend cap documented for message posting frequency.
No rate or quota limits are documented for add_note calls.
Artifacts do not describe any record of what the hosted sync service received or when, beyond the agent's own (undocumented) logs.
This element represents external recipients of posted messages, not an authenticating peer presenting identity to the agent; agent-identity spoofing is covered under proc.mcp_slack instead.
This inbound flow carries tool metadata from the server to the agent and does not itself carry confidential data outward; the disclosure occurs via df.notes_add_egress instead.
Artifacts do not describe size or rate limits on tool definition payloads returned by quicknotes_mcp.
Artifacts do not show the content of notes_output responses beyond the add_note tool description, so tamper risk on returned content cannot be assessed.
Artifacts do not specify what information quicknotes_mcp returns in call results beyond the add_note argument exfiltration already covered by F1.
No documented limits on response size or call frequency from this server.

rating.rationale: Inherent risk is critical: quicknotes_mcp's unpinned, individually published tool description (in.tool_definitions, untrusted) instructs the agent to read ~/.aws/credentials (cap.file_read, restricted data) and forward it through add_note (cap.notes_add) to the author's third-party hosted sync service -- an untrusted source reaching an irreversible, confidential-data egress sink (U x S3), matching the lethal trifecta pattern (TC1). The declared A2-style control (approval on first call, then remembered 'always allow') is never wired to any capability's approval_gate_ref and is remembered rather than re-checked, so under control_decay.md it earns no residual credit; no egress allowlist, credential scoping, destination confirmation, definition pinning, or audit logging exists, so residual stays critical (F1). Three further property findings round out the picture: unrestricted Slack posting to any channel including external organizations (F2, high), no attributable audit trail for agent actions (F3, high), and no step/runtime limits bounding unattended operation (F4, high). A forecast-only finding (F5) notes that the identical unpinned @latest pattern applies to the filesystem and Slack MCP servers, so a future package update to either could open an equivalent critical path even though no poisoning is evidenced there today. Forecast risk remains critical because F1's residual is already at the ceiling; the single gap that most drives both the present and forecast picture is the absence of tool-definition pinning combined with a real, non-remembered raw-action approval gate on egress-capable tools.

limitations: This assessment reflects the declared design and configuration shown in mcp.json, the quicknotes_mcp tools/list excerpt, and the provided runtime notes, not observed runtime behavior of the deployed agent.

No system prompt or agent instructions were provided, so goal-hijack susceptibility is assessed only through the tool-description injection vector found in quicknotes_mcp; other injection surfaces in the agent's own instructions cannot be ruled in or out.

No evidence was provided about quicknotes_mcp's actual tool-call return content (in.notes_output) beyond the add_note description, so risk on that specific flow is recorded as not_assessed rather than as a finding.

Autonomy is taken as declared (first-call approval, then remembered 'always allow'); no runtime logs were available to confirm how often approvals are actually requested or granted, so approval_volume could not be determined and is treated as absent of credit per the remembered-approval rule.
